title: Selling to Businesses: Accounts, Contract Prices, Quotes and Approvals
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/21-b2b-commerce/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (a roadmap paragraph, p05, and a conclusion paragraph that answers the opening, p47); these are listed in decision_log.

know: The B2B object model the platforms share (an organization with locations, people and roles, with prices, assortments and terms attached to the organization or location) and the differences from a consumer purchase: contract and tiered prices excluding VAT, quotes, payment terms, credit limits, pre-season orders and the buyer's own approval rules.
The price layers (list, tier, contract, quote), the rule that the most specific wins, and why a quote freezes the price the order and the invoice use.

The four ways to give business customers a channel (a B2C platform's B2B features, a dedicated B2B platform, an ERP-driven web store, the buyer's own system through EDI or punchout) and where each fits.
believe: The ERP owns the money facts (company identity, wholesale and contract prices, payment terms, credit limits, invoices) and publishes them; the platform owns the session facts (logins, roles, the buyer's approval rules).
The share of wholesale orders keyed in by hand measures the facts the portal cannot see: it is a list of missing integrations, not of missing features.
can_do: Write the ownership table for the company account, contacts, prices, quotes, terms and credit, approval rules, orders and invoices at their own company.

Decide whether a credit check at order placement should ask the ERP synchronously or accept the order and hold it, and choose among the four channel options by the buyers and the facts the checkout needs.

audience.who: Newcomers who have joined a brand, wholesaler, manufacturer or commerce vendor with a business-customer channel; most of all the engineer or architect asked to 'move wholesale onto the portal', who must decide what the portal reads from the ERP. Product managers choosing between a consumer platform's B2B features and a dedicated B2B platform come next.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 incidents in outline and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II and III: product, variant, SKU and GTIN with one owning system per attribute; prices selected once at order placement and frozen, dated copies compared daily; available-to-promise and per-channel buffers; checkout creating the order once; one order record with three status lines; tax from three facts, one invoice per shipment, credit notes as the only correction.

From the previous chapter: a marketplace connector owns nothing, each channel gets one available-to-promise figure, and every marketplace order is created in the order record under the marketplace's id.
does_not_know: Company account, contact, location, roles; contract pricing, tiered pricing, customer-specific assortment; prices excluding VAT for business buyers.
Quote, quote validity, draft order; payment terms (net 30), credit limit, open balance, credit check; the buyer's approval workflow, budgets and cost centers.
Pre-season and in-season orders; punchout, cXML, OCI; B2B2C; ERP-driven web store; Peppol.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a steady share of e-mailed wholesale orders, the reader names the facts the portal cannot see and the integrations that would bring those orders in, not a new B2B platform.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's B2B portal takes 62% of its wholesale orders; the rest arrive by e-mail or phone and are keyed into the ERP, and that share has not fallen in two years. The larger accounts have pre-season discounts agreed per account, and finance holds some portal orders by hand a day after they are placed. Using only this chapter: why do these buyers keep e-mailing, and what would bring their orders into the portal?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The portal cannot see what they agreed or what they owe: pre-season and contract prices live in the ERP's customer price lists and in e-mail, credit is checked only in the ERP at order entry, and portal and keyed orders are two records. Publish contract and pre-season price lists from the ERP as price events with effective dates into each account's catalog; check credit at placement against the ERP's open balance, synchronously if the ERP answers fast enough or by accepting and holding the order with an event-driven release; create every wholesale order, however it arrives, in one order record. Missing integrations, not missing features.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an invoice priced from a changed price list after a quote was accepted, the reader names the rule that was broken and the design that prevents it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A business buyer accepts a quote at a negotiated price; before the goods ship, the seasonal price list changes, and the invoice shows the new list price. Using only this chapter: what went wrong, and how should quotes, orders and invoices be designed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A quote freezes the price: it is stored as an object with a validity date, the order is created from it, and the invoice is generated from what shipped at the price the order carried, never recomputed from the current price list. Which price layer wins (most specific: quote over contract over tier over list) is written down and implemented once in the pricing source, so the portal, the order and the invoice compute the same price.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say whether a punchout cart is an order and where the eventual order goes.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: a corporate buyer's procurement system opens the supplier's shop, the buyer fills a cart, and the cart returns to the procurement system. Is that an order, and where should the eventual order be created?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No: the cart is a requisition returned to the buyer's procurement system for its own approval. The order arrives later as a cXML OrderRequest or an EDI ORDERS and is created in the same order record as a portal order, with the buyer's purchase order number as its uniqueness key.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What differs when the buyer is a company (accounts with several people and locations, negotiated prices, quantity breaks, payment terms, credit limits, approvals, pre-season orders); which records every B2B platform needs; who should own the company account, contacts, prices, terms, credit and orders; the choices for building a wholesale channel; independent shops ordering from Kestrel & Pine through its portal or by e-mail, with Bergzicht's EDI orders left to the next chapter. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's wholesale figures and the platforms' B2B documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What is different when the buyer is a company?
thesis.claim: When the buyer is a company, the customer is an organization with locations, people and roles, the price is a stack of dated agreements, and payment is terms within a credit limit. A portal can replace e-mail and phone orders only if it reads those agreements at checkout from the system that owns them (the ERP for terms, credit and wholesale prices) and every wholesale order, however it arrives, is created in one order record.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that B2B is a feature set to switch on: a platform's company accounts, price lists and net terms let business customers order like consumers, the share still ordering by e-mail or phone reflects buyers' habits or features the portal lacks, and the remedy is a richer B2B platform.
thesis.so_what: In 2026, 38% of Kestrel & Pine's 9,400 wholesale orders were keyed into the ERP by hand, a share unchanged since 2024, because the larger accounts' pre-season terms lived in the ERP's customer price lists, the portal could not check credit, and portal and keyed orders were two records. On 25 February 2027 De Kaap Buitensport e-mailed a pre-season order worth €6,384 because the portal showed €6,720 at list, and the ERP held it over its €15,000 credit limit until Lea Moreau approved it by e-mail. A merchant that accepts the claim decides who owns the company account, the price and the credit limit before it chooses or configures a B2B platform, and reads its keyed-order share as a list of missing integrations.
thesis.how_why: Every platform can hold company accounts, price lists, terms and credit, so when nobody names an owner each system keeps its own copy and the copies drift. A wholesale invoice must match the price the buyer was shown for the same date and quantity, so the layering rule (quote over contract over tier over list) and the frozen quote are implemented once in the pricing source and published with effective dates. What a customer owes is known only to receivables, so a credit check against a nightly copy accepts orders finance later holds, and a portal that cannot check credit sends larger orders back to e-mail, where the ERP checks them at entry. Orders that enter through different doors land in different systems unless all are created in one record keyed on the buyer's purchase order number.

supporting_claims.claim: A business buyer is an organization with locations, people and roles, to which prices, assortments, payment terms and a credit limit are attached, and every major platform models it that way under different names.

Every platform can hold the company account, the prices and the credit, so each fact needs one named owner: the ERP owns the money facts (company identity, wholesale and contract prices, terms, credit, invoices) and publishes them as events; the platform owns the session facts (logins, roles, the buyer's approval rules).

A B2B price is a stack of dated layers (list, tier, contract, quote) in which the most specific wins; the rule is implemented once in the pricing source, and a quote freezes the price the order and the invoice use.

Payment terms and the credit limit are receivables facts, so the credit check at order placement asks the ERP, synchronously or by accepting and holding the order with an event-driven release, never a nightly copy; the buyer's own approval rules are the opposite control and live in the platform.

The four ways to give business customers a channel (a consumer platform's B2B features, a dedicated B2B platform, an ERP-driven web store, the buyer's own system through EDI or punchout) fit different buyers and differ in which system answers at checkout; whichever is chosen, every wholesale order is created in one order record keyed on the buyer's purchase order number.
The share of wholesale orders keyed in by hand counts the facts the portal cannot see, so it is a list of missing integrations, not of missing features.

role.contribution: Gives the part its business buyers: the agreements (prices, terms, credit) the checkout must read from the ERP that owns them, one order record for portal, keyed, EDI and punchout orders, and the keyed-order share as the measure of what the portal cannot see.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene: the 38% and the three reasons behind it, then W2

flow.rationale: The 38% comes first so every term arrives as part of explaining why those orders are keyed by hand. What differs for a business buyer comes next because it names the objects (account, price, terms, credit, approvals) that every later section assigns or checks. Ownership follows because the price and credit sections then explain facts whose owner the reader already knows; the price layers precede credit because a credit check adds the new order's value, built from those layers, to the open balance before comparing it with the limit; the flow requirements follow both, because they move the facts those sections explain. The choices come once the reader knows which facts the checkout must read, because each option is defined by where those facts live; the stages say which option fits when, and the recommendation comes at their end, once the reader knows both the options and Kestrel & Pine's stage. The worked order follows the choices so that its after-Waypoint column shows the recommendation's three integrations at work, and the failures come last because each is read against the rule that prevents it. Moving ownership after pricing and credit would leave both sections without the owner they rely on; moving the choices before ownership would compare options by features, the view the thesis disputes.

advances_thesis.how: States the ownership rule and the requirements each flow must meet, with the credit check as the decisive one.

flow.rationale: The conflict, then the connector documentation that names it and the platforms that leave it open, then the ownership table, then the pattern it shows; the pattern can only be read off a table the reader has seen. The flow requirements wait until the price and credit sections have explained the facts they move.

sections.heading: Credit, Terms and the Buyer's Own Controls
sections.controlling_idea: Payment terms and the credit limit are the seller's receivables facts, which the ERP owns and the checkout must check against today's balance at order placement, while the buyer's approval workflow is the buyer's own control, held in the platform.

advances_thesis.how: Defines terms, credit and approvals and says which system holds and checks each.

flow.rationale: The seller's two controls, terms then credit, because the credit check uses the open balance the terms create, then the buyer's control as the contrast.

transition_in.carries_over: The price an order carries.
transition_in.introduces: How and when the buyer pays for it, and who may let it through.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Payment terms say when the buyer must pay and must be stored as structured data with a trigger; the ERP owns the invoice date and tracks what is overdue, and the platform needs a copy to show the agreement and let the buyer order without a card.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A merchant that sells to businesses has four realistic ways to give them a channel, chosen less by features than by who the buyers are and which system can answer at checkout.

The first option, a consumer platform's B2B features, adds company accounts, buyer-specific catalogs and payment terms to the platform that serves consumers and reuses its catalog and checkout, if it can represent the agreements.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The B2B channel outgrows the platform's features not when the account count grows but when the facts the checkout needs stop living in the platform; for Kestrel & Pine those facts can be published into the platform, so the author recommends staying with its B2B features and adding three integrations.

advances_thesis.how: Shows which channel design each stage needs, reads the keyed share as the signal, and recommends the integrations that answer it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author recommends that a brand like Kestrel & Pine keep the platform's B2B features and fix the three gaps behind the 38%: ERP price events for contract and pre-season lists, a credit check at placement against the ERP's open balance, and every wholesale order created in the OMS, provided the ERP exposes prices and balances by API.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The outdoor shop of the opening, De Kaap's held order and the 38% are one problem: every platform can store the agreement, and what decides whether a business buyer uses the portal is whether the checkout reads price, terms and credit from the ERP that owns them and creates the order in the one record every wholesale order shares.
conclusion.so_what: The remedy for a keyed-order share is integration work on the platform already in place (prices published from the ERP, a credit check at placement, one order record), not a richer B2B platform.

callback.to: The opening's outdoor shop ordering sixty jackets at a negotiated price, on thirty-day terms, within a credit limit.
callback.how: Paragraph p47 says what the checkout must read for that shop's order to go through the portal, and reads the 38% as the count of orders where it did not.

takeaway.content: Write the ownership table for your own company account, prices, terms and credit, count the wholesale orders keyed by hand and name the missing fact behind each reason, and take the eight questions to your own channel.

hand_off.carries_over: The wholesale portal as the self-service path of the business channel, and the fourth channel option this chapter only named: the buyer's own system, sending EDI orders or punching out.
hand_off.introduces: The documents the largest buyers send and expect (order, despatch advice, invoice), the system each must come from, and the e-invoicing mandates that now reach business invoices.
